passage:
On Thursday, Dhruv told his mother Disha that his science project would take ten minutes and he would begin after dinner on Friday. "It's only a chart," he said. On Friday night he found he had to cut out pictures, look up three facts and colour the border. At half past nine he was still gluing, and the chart had gone crooked.

Earlier that week, Dhruv had promised his father Uday, "I'll draw the mango in five minutes, then we can go to the park." Uday looked at the clock. An hour later Dhruv was still shading the leaves, absorbed and surprised. "Is it evening already?" he asked. He had not been trying to fool anyone. He truly thought five minutes was enough.

On Saturday, Uday sat with him and wrote next to each task how long the last one had taken. Dhruv stared at the list and said, "Oh. It's not ten minutes, it's more like an hour."

qa.q: How long did Dhruv say his science project would take?
qa.a: Dhruv said the project would take ten minutes.

qa.q: What do the science chart and the mango drawing have in common?
qa.a: In both Dhruv gives a short time, ten minutes for the chart and five for the mango, and then finds it takes far longer, because he pictures the ideal path and has little sense of how long things take, so his promises are sincere but unreliable.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he asked whether it was evening already?
qa.a: Dhruv felt surprised and absorbed, honestly unaware that an hour had gone.

qa.q: What could Uday do to help Dhruv plan time better?
qa.a: Uday could do what he did, writing down how long each task really took, so Dhruv can compare guesses with real times.

grounding: The planning fallacy in a child: promising short times for a project and a drawing and being surprised by how much longer they take.
